newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens sees flat profits in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Siemens sees flat profits in 1996/97.

text.p: German industrial group Siemens AG on Monday stood by an earlier forecast of flat profit in 1996/97, even though net income rose three percent in the year's first nine months, exceeding analysts expectations.

Losses in its medical and transportation units and higher taxes would dampen net profit -- although sales for the full year would climb seven percent to more than 100 billion marks, CEO Heinrich von Pierer said at a news conference.
He said profit would rise again in 1997/98, with Siemens aiming to lift its return on equity to 15 percent by 2000, up from an expected 10 percent in the year ending September 30.
"In contrast to the current year, we expect a significant rise in (1998/99) net income, one that will be notably higher than the growth in business volume," he said.
Some analysts agreed a profit rise was near. "I think earnings will accelerate," Credit Lyonnais's Andreas Wahl said. "I think the company will make more efforts to improve profit."
Others, such as Kevin Brau at CS First Boston, have criticised Siemens for restructuring too slowly, while Moody's Investor Service recently called the efforts "insufficient.".
Siemens shares have risen about 20 percent in the last month and traded at 111.40 marks at 1054 GMT on Monday, down 7.45 marks.

For the first nine months of 1996/97, Siemens reported sales of 71.2 billion marks, beating Wahl's forecast of 67.9 billion marks. Net income for the period also surpassed his prediction of 1.68 billion marks.
Nine month orders increased 14 percent to 82.8 billion marks. Siemens said favourable currency rates added two percent to its nine month sales and four percent to order totals.
For the full year, Siemens expected orders to rise to more than 106 billion marks. But exchange rates would not have an impact on profit, CFO Karl-Hermann Baumann told Reuters.

"For the time being we are maintaining our (1996/97 after-tax) forecast in the range of 2.5 billion marks, the same as last year," with a rise in pretax profit offset by higher tax liabilities, he said.
Baumann said the Siemens-Nixdorf Informationssystems AG computer unit would nearly double profit this year to over 100 million marks from 52 million in 1995/96.
The public and private communicaitons groups would also report "profit above expectations," he said.
SNI and the public and private communications units each saw double-digit growth in nine-month sales.

At the same time, the medical and transportation technology units would each report losses of over 100 million marks due to restructuring costs and price pressure. The medical business would show a clear profit next year, but transportaiton would take another year to reach profitability, Baumann said.
The company's semiconductor unit, previously one of its most profitable, also remained under pressure from falling memory chip prices and high investments in new plants.

Von Pierer added that Siemens was not going to sell the medical unit. "It is an indispensable part of our core business, he said. Siemens wanted to sell the medical unit's dental equipment business "to optimise the entire group and is by no means a first step toward divestment."
Siemens also expected to complete the sale of its defense electronics business late this year, after receiving firm bids in August from buyers including Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG, Baumann said.

The company was also reorganising its industrial businesses, and SNI was splitting off its service business into five separate operating companies -- all in an effort to lift profit. SNI expected to lose 58 million marks on services this year, and then turn a profit of 30 million marks next year.

Geographically, Siemens saw strong international growth in the nine months to June 30, with North and South American orders rising 26 percent to 16.5 billion marks and Asian orders up 45 percent to 11.5 billion marks.
German orders fell two percent to 27.2 billion marks, although orders in the rest of Europe increased 13 percent to 22.9 billion marks.
